images.title: Bhinna, the broken whole
images.purpose: Show that in ancient India a fraction was called bhinna, meaning broken, and was written with the numerator above the denominator and no line between them.
images.composition: One plain old page card on the left and one roti broken into two equal halves on the right, with wide space between, and one name line centred below.
images.exact_structure: Left: one plain flat cream rectangle with a thin dark outline, like an old page, holding only the digit 1 written directly above the digit 2 in large dark text, with no line between them. A small caption sits under the card. Right: one flat round roti broken along its diameter into exactly 2 equal halves, pulled slightly apart with a small gap; the left half is filled teal #0072B2, the right half plain. Below, centred: two short lines. No people, no map, no timeline. Exactly 1 card, 1 roti, 2 halves.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
a line or slash drawn between the 1 and the 2 on the old page
images.takeaway: A fraction was called bhinna: a broken whole.
images.description: An old page shows one half written as 1 above 2 with no line, as in ancient India around 300 CE; beside it a roti broken into 2 equal halves, with the names bhinna, meaning broken, and bhaga or ansha, meaning part or piece.
images.context: Shown with the concept as its one key picture, next to the walkthrough video. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to point at the old page, read the fraction aloud, and say what is missing compared with how we write it today.

image_decisions.why: The old way of writing a fraction and the meaning of bhinna are both visual; one clean picture carries them.
